newsitem.title: USA: Republicans claim mantle of America's majority.
newsitem.headline: Republicans claim mantle of America's majority.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
"We are the majority party of America," outgoing Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour claimed in a recent speech.
Democrats say that is nonsense, especially after last November's presidential election in which they won the White House for the second time in a row.
So who's right?

Barbour based his claim on the fact that Republicans not only control both houses of Congress but also provide 32 of the country's 50 state governors including major states like California, Texas, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Michigan.

"We're the majority party on Capitol Hill and in the statehouses. But more important, we're the majority party in ideas," Barbour told the Republican National Committee in his farewell speech last week.
"The majority of Americans agree with our ideas -- with our dedication to smaller, smarter government, to lower taxes, to balancing the budget and to reforming welfare."
But the newly elected Democratic Party general chairman, Colorado Gov. Roy Romer, sees the parties at a rough parity.

"We won the (presidential) election. That ought to be the first answer. We captured some congressional seats. We captured some state legislatures back," he told Reuters. "This thing goes back and forth like a pendulum. I think the parties are in close competition."

Romer's predecessor as chairman, Connecticut Sen. Christopher Dodd, put forward another argument for Democratic supremacy, noting that Republican support was strongest among white Protestant Americans, especially men, while Democrats enjoyed wider support from women, Catholics and minorities.
"One of the great hallmarks of this party is our diversity. We look like America. That's what distinguishes us more than anything else from the other party," Dodd said.
Barbour tacitly acknowledged the point, calling in his speech for Republicans to reach out more effectively to women and to ethnic minorities.

The perception of which party actually represents the majority of Americans has importance beyond mere bragging rights. It may also govern the way the parties handle internal dissent and project themselves to voters.

Barbour said Republicans ought to start behaving like a majority instead of a beleagured minority. They had to learn how to tolerate diversity and accept internal debate and dissent, even over painful issues like abortion.

It is generally accepted that the Democrats were the majority party for several decades starting in the 1930s. While Republicans often held the presidency in those years, Democrats maintained an iron grip on Congress for most of the time and dominated a majority of state legislatures. They ran several like virtual one-party states.
That era is obviously over. But has it given way to a new era of Republican dominance?

Not really, said Gary Jacobson, a political scientist with the University of California, San Diego. "The Republicans are now at competitive equality. They may have a very slight edge in congressional elections but they just lost the presidency twice. The big picture is, it's pretty even," he said.

What is undeniable is that the ideological centre of gravity in American politics has moved to the right. That means Republicans have become more conservative while Democrats, led by President Clinton, are increasingly moving into the political centre.
"The Republicans' move to the right is their Achilles heel, particularly in presidential elections," Jacobson said.

But with public cynicism with politicians at an all-time high, neither party can count on the kind of permanent loyalty they once enjoyed. The country may be in for a seesaw period with neither party forming a permanent majority.
